4. Performance Evaluation

benjination2@gmail.com • 7/29/2026

Performance Evaluation of Dolphin ICS SISCI API
Three-Node PCIe Interconnect System
Empirical Benchmark Results, Deployment Challenges, and Analysis
Part 3 of Research Series
Benjamin Niccum
University of Texas at Arlington
CSE 5393 - Directed Research
March 2026
Abstract
This performance evaluation is the third document in a research series on Dolphin PCIe
fabric technology for neighborhood-scale decentralized networks. Prior documents covered the
literature review and system architecture design. This report presents empirical benchmark
results from the implemented three-node system, along with a detailed account of the hardware
and software challenges overcome during deployment.
This report presents empirical performance measurements from a three-node Dolphin ICS
SISCI system implementing the architecture detailed in the companion design document.
A dedicated section documents the system integration process, including a failed Windows
platform attempt, PCIe BAR resource allocation conflicts requiring Linux-only deployment,
driver stack configuration challenges, and software bugs resolved during first end-to-end
operation. Five benchmark applications then evaluate critical performance domains: DMA-
based file transfer, remote memory access latency, transparent memory access, interrupt
signaling round-trip latency, and a live fabric monitoring dashboard.
The evaluation quantifies actual system performance by measuring throughput, latency,
CPU overhead, and consistency across multiple test iterations on a star topology with ghost
(Node 1, fabric ID 12) as the hub and DolphinBenny1 (Node 2, fabric ID 8) and Dolphin-
Benny2 (Node 3, fabric ID 4) as leaf nodes connected via dual x4 links. Results demon-
strate the practical capabilities and operating characteristics of PCIe fabric technology in
distributed computing applications, providing data-driven insights for system optimization
and application development.
Key findings: DMA bulk transfer sustained 7.163 GB/s on average across five runs (peak
7.167 GB/s), consistent with the PCIe 4.0 x4 per-link bandwidth ceiling (∼7.88 GB/s) after
ghost’s CPU upgrade. RDMA PIO reads demonstrated a mean latency of 1.724 µs with
a consistent p99 of 2.000 µs across 1,000 iterations — run-to-run standard deviation of
0.076 µs across five runs. Transparent memory cycles (write + flush + read) averaged
1.978 µs, only 0.254 µs above bare RDMA. Interrupt round-trip latency averaged 30.688 µs
in steady state, with a best-case floor of 20 µs and p99 values ranging from 360–436 µs across
runs. Analysis synthesizes the empirical results, identifies observable system constraints, and
provides practical deployment guidance.

1 Introduction Dolphin PCIe Benchmark
1 Introduction
This performance evaluation report is the third component of a comprehensive research se-
ries examining Dolphin PCIe fabric technology for neighborhood-scale decentralized computing
networks. This document builds directly upon two prior works:
1. Literature Review - “Dolphin PCIe Fabric Technology: Foundations for Neighborhood-
Scale Decentralized Data Networks” (January 2026), which established the theoretical
foundations, technology background, and market context for PCIe fabric interconnects
2. Architecture Design - “Three-Node PCIe Fabric Demonstration System” (February
2026), which detailed the complete system architecture, hardware specifications, and im-
plementation plan for the test platform
1.1 Report Scope and Purpose
While the literature review provided theoretical context and the architecture design specified the
system configuration, this report covers two complementary topics. First, it documents the sys-
tem deployment and integration process — the hardware compatibility decisions, driver
configuration challenges, and software bugs that were encountered and resolved between initial
hardware insertion and stable three-node operation. Second, it presents empirical perfor-
mance measurements from the operational system, summarizes the measured performance
characteristics, and provides data-driven insights for optimization and practical deployment.
This document deliberately avoids repeating background information on SISCI API fun-
damentals, hardware architecture details, or market applications, as those topics are compre-
hensively covered in the companion documents. Readers seeking system architecture details,
hardware specifications, or theoretical background should consult the respective prior docu-
ments.
1.2 Evaluation Objectives
The primary objectives of this performance evaluation are:
1. Document Deployment Reality: Record the practical challenges of deploying a PCIe
fabric system on consumer-class hardware outside a controlled datacenter environment
2. Quantify Actual Performance: Measure real-world latency, throughput, and overhead
across five benchmark domains
3. Characterize Measured Behavior: Summarize the observed latency, throughput, con-
sistency, and overhead of the implemented system
4. Identify Performance Characteristics: Determine optimal use cases, bottlenecks, and
scaling behavior
5. Provide Implementation Guidance: Document practical lessons learned for future
deployments
1.3 System Topology
The operational system is a three-node star configuration. Ghost (Node 1, fabric ID 12) serves
as the central hub and runs the JavaFX monitoring GUI. DolphinBenny1 (Node 2, fabric ID
8) and DolphinBenny2 (Node 3, fabric ID 4) are leaf nodes connected exclusively to ghost via
dual PCIe copper cables (x4×2 per remote node). DolphinBenny1 and DolphinBenny2 have
no direct fabric path to each other; inter-node traffic between them must traverse ghost. All
benchmarks in this report exercise direct ghost-to-remote connections.

1.4 Benchmark Applications
Five purpose-built C applications exercise specific SISCI API capabilities:
• File Transfer Demo (FTD): Evaluates DMA-based bulk transfer throughput with
128 MB transfers using hardware-offloaded SCIStartDmaTransfer
• Remote Memory Demo (RMD): Characterizes fine-grained RDMA operation latency
across 1,000 iterations
• Transparency Demo (TD): Assesses transparent shared memory programming model
overhead across 100 mixed local/remote operation cycles
• Interrupt Demo (ID): Measures hardware interrupt round-trip latency across 100 iter-
ations using SCITriggerDataInterrupt and SCIWaitForDataInterrupt
• Fabric Drive (FD): Demonstrates POSIX filesystem access over PCIe fabric via a FUSE-
based virtual drive backed by remote shared memory, mounted at /tmp/dolphin-fabric
The four quantitative benchmarks report latency and throughput metrics; the Fabric Drive
serves as a functionality demonstration confirming that standard filesystem operations work
transparently over the PCIe fabric. The following sections present the deployment challenges,
methodology, results, and analysis of these applications.
2 System Deployment and Integration
Deploying a three-node PCIe fabric cluster using consumer-class hardware and a niche in-
terconnect technology presented a series of non-trivial hardware and software challenges. This
section documents the integration process in chronological order, from initial hardware insertion
through final three-node operation. Understanding these deployment obstacles is as important
as the benchmark results themselves, as they reveal the practical prerequisites for operating
Dolphin SISCI systems on non-datacenter Linux platforms.
2.1 Platform Selection and PCIe Compatibility Assessment
The first candidate machine for a remote Dolphin node was an HP OmniDesk M02-0127c desktop
running Windows 11. Although the MXH930 card was electrically recognized by the system
(three VEN 11F8 PCIe devices enumerated in Device Manager and WinRE), the machine was
ultimately determined to be incompatible as a Dolphin node, for two independent reasons.
2.1.1 Secure Boot and Option ROM Rejection
With Secure Boot enabled in the factory BIOS configuration, inserting the MXH930 card caused
the machine to refuse to POST. The UEFI firmware blocked the card’s Option ROM signature.
Disabling Secure Boot resolved the POST failure but introduced a secondary problem: Bit-
Locker’s Trusted Platform Module (TPM) measurement of the firmware changed, triggering a
BitLocker recovery key prompt on the next Windows boot. The recovery key was retrieved and
applied, and BitLocker protectors were suspended for subsequent reboots using manage-bde
-protectors -disable C: -RebootCount 3.
Page 6
2 System Deployment and Integration Dolphin PCIe Benchmark
2.1.2 PCIe BAR / NVMe MMIO Collision
With Secure Boot disabled, the Dolphin Express MX v5.25.1 Windows driver was installed
(Cluster Node component; driver file dis mx sio.sys confirmed present and registered). How-
ever, on every subsequent boot, Windows produced an INACCESSIBLE BOOT DEVICE (Stop code
0x7B) blue screen. The failure occurred at the earliest phases of kernel initialization — before
Safe Mode driver loading, before any user-space recovery options, and even with bcdedit /set
{default} safeboot minimal applied.
Diagnosis using bootrec /scanos from the Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE) re-
turned zero Windows installations — the NVMe boot device was completely invisible to the
firmware when the MXH930 card was present.
A comparative lspci analysis on a Linux machine with the same Dolphin card revealed the
root cause: the MXH930 Region 4 BAR allocates 64 MB at address 0xb0000000, displacing
the NVMe controller’s MMIO address assignment. Specifically, inserting the card shifted the
NVMe controller from PCI slot 01:00.0 to 04:00.0, reassigning all downstream bus numbers
by three. Windows had been installed — and had recorded the boot device path — without
the card present. On reboot with the card installed, Windows could not locate the NVMe at
its recorded address.
The HP M02-0127c consumer BIOS provides no mechanism to control Above-4G Decoding,
Resizable BAR assignment, or individual PCIe slot MMIO ranges. All attempted remediation
strategies failed:
• bcdedit /set {default} truncatememory 0x100000000 — Windows 11 ignores this
parameter
• bcdedit /set {default} pciexpress forcedisable — disables PCIe Active State Power
Management (ASPM) only; has no effect on BAR allocation
• bootrec /fixboot — returned Access Denied (a Windows 11 Secure Boot side-effect
even after Secure Boot was disabled)
• Registry key PciAssignBusNumbers = 1 applied from Linux via chntpw — survived Win-
dows auto-repair; did not change boot behavior
• BCD editing via chntpw from Linux — segfaulted on the BCD hive, a known upstream
bug in that tool
Linux is inherently immune to this failure mode: the pci=realloc kernel parameter causes
the Linux kernel to reassign all PCIe BAR allocations independently of firmware-provided re-
source maps on every boot, so the NVMe is discovered at its current address regardless of what
the BIOS or firmware originally assigned.
A detailed bug report was filed with Dolphin Interconnect Solutions (support contact: Simen
Thoresen), documenting the PCIe bus enumeration shift, all remediation attempts, and a com-
plete lspci device-tree comparison with and without the card. Dolphin confirmed this failure
scenario had not been previously reported and noted that reinstalling Windows with the card
already present — so that Windows records the NVMe at its post-insertion address 04:00.0
— would produce a working but non-portable installation that would break again if the card
were removed.
Decision: Linux-only deployment. All three nodes run Linux exclusively. No further
Windows compatibility work was pursued.

2.2 Linux Driver Installation and Service Stack Configuration
2.2.1 GRUB Bootloader Heap Corruption
On the machine designated DolphinBenny2 (AMD Ryzen, Linux Mint / Ubuntu 24.04 HWE
kernel), inserting the MXH930 card before installing the Dolphin driver caused GRUB to fail
during boot with:
alloc magic is broken at 0x40bb750: 0
This is GRUB heap corruption caused by the MXH930 card’s BAR allocations overlapping
the memory region GRUB uses during early boot. The fix is straightforward on Linux: adding
pci=realloc to the kernel command line causes the Linux kernel — not GRUB — to handle
all PCIe resource assignment, bypassing the BIOS-provided allocation that caused the collision.
The parameter swiotlb=65536 was added simultaneously to ensure DMA buffer space is al-
located at IOMMU boundaries required for the Dolphin DMA engine. Both parameters were
written to /etc/default/grub and applied with sudo update-grub. After this change, the
system booted correctly with the card installed.
2.2.2 HWE Kernel Version and Installer Compatibility
The Dolphin eXpressWare v5.25.1 standard installer rejected DolphinBenny2’s HWE kernel
version via a distribution version check. The workaround was to invoke the installer with the
--skip-distro-check flag, bypassing the kernel string comparison. Following installation, all
five required Dolphin kernel modules and their corresponding systemd services were confirmed
operational:
dis kosif →dis irm →dis mx dma →dis mx ntb →dis sisci
These services must start in dependency order. If any service in the chain fails, all down-
stream services remain inactive. The dis sisci service — the top-level SISCI API endpoint
— was the most sensitive to upstream failures.
2.2.3 SISCI Host Configuration File (dishosts.conf)
The Dolphin software stack requires a correctly formed /etc/dis/dishosts.conf file on each
node to discover other nodes on the fabric. Two configuration errors were encountered:
1. Placeholder hostname: The default configuration file contains DIS HOSTNAME LOCAL as
a template placeholder rather than the actual system hostname. Leaving this unreplaced
caused dis sisci to fail at startup with a node resolution error.
2. Block ordering constraint: The dishosts.conf parser requires all HOSTNAME: and
ADAPTER: definitions to appear before any SOCKETADAPTER: block. Violating this order-
ing causes the parser to silently ignore the misplaced entries without emitting an error,
producing a partially-functional or non-functional fabric configuration.
After correcting both issues and restarting the service chain, fabric connectivity was verified
with dis diag and disinfo -hostnames.
2.2.4 WiFi Regression After Kernel Upgrade
The machine designated ghost (Node 1) required a kernel upgrade to 6.17.0-19-generic to
support the Dolphin kernel modules. After this upgrade, the onboard Intel AX200 WiFi adapter
stopped functioning. The cause was that the new kernel package did not include the updated
iwlwifi firmware required by the AX200. The fix was sudo apt install linux-firmware,
which restores the firmware files needed by the Intel wireless driver.

2.3 Network Topology and Fabric Configuration
The final three-node topology is a star configuration with dual-link connections from ghost
to each remote node (Figure 1). Ghost (Node 1, fabric ID 12) is the only multi-port node.
DolphinBenny1 (Node 2, fabric ID 8) and DolphinBenny2 (Node 3, fabric ID 4) each connect
exclusively to ghost via two PCIe copper cables, yielding dual x4 links (designated x4×2) per
remote node pair.

Figure 1: Three-node star topology: ghost is the sole hub; each remote node connects via dual
x4 links. DolphinBenny1 and DolphinBenny2 have no direct fabric path to each other.
This topology was chosen because the two remote nodes each contain only a two-port subset
of the MXH930’s port array in their available PCIe expansion slots, while ghost’s full four-port
card accommodates both connections simultaneously.
An important consequence of the star topology is that communication between Dolphin-
Benny1 and DolphinBenny2 must traverse ghost as an intermediate node. All benchmark
applications in this evaluation exercise direct ghost-to-remote connections only, which represent
the primary use case for this configuration.
2.4 Software Integration Challenges
2.4.1 Java Virtual Machine Flag Incompatibility
The monitoring GUI is a Java 21 / JavaFX application built with Maven. During development
an additional JVM flag — --sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access=allow — was added to the
javafx-maven-plugin configuration to suppress a runtime warning. This flag was introduced
in Java 23 and is unrecognized by any earlier JVM. On a machine running OpenJDK 21.0.10,
the JVM exited immediately at launch with:
Unrecognized option: --sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access=allow
Error: Could not create the Java Virtual Machine.
The flag was removed from pom.xml; only --enable-native-access=javafx.graphics,ALL-UNNAMED
was retained.
2.4.2 Concurrent Branch Development and Merge Conflict in Metrics Agent
The SISCI metrics pipeline — which provides live CPU, memory, and disk data from Nodes 2
and 3 to the GUI — underwent two architectural iterations. The first design published metrics
into a 4 KB SISCI segment (ID 600) using a C struct node metrics t defined in a shared
header. A second design introduced during parallel development used a 2 MB segment (ID 500)
and a restructured struct (NodeMetricsData) with an explicit magic-number validity field
(0xD01F1171).
Page 9
2 System Deployment and Integration Dolphin PCIe Benchmark
Both designs were developed concurrently without proper branch isolation. When the
branches were merged, metrics agent.c and Makefile were left with unresolved conflict mark-
ers (<<<<<<< HEAD /======= / >>>>>>>), preventing compilation entirely. The conflict was
resolved by adopting the segment-500 / NodeMetricsData design throughout, as it matched the
contemporaneous metrics reader.c implementation. An additional improvement was made
during resolution: the original single-sample /proc/stat CPU measurement was replaced with
a two-sample delta, producing accurate utilization values rather than instantaneous raw coun-
ters. Explicit SCISetSegmentAvailable / SCISetSegmentUnavailable calls were also added
for proper SISCI segment lifecycle management.
2.4.3 PIO vs. DMA for Bandwidth Measurement
The initial bandwidth measurement in metrics reader performed a CPU-side memcpy directly
into the mapped remote segment virtual address, followed by an SCIFlush call. This is Pro-
grammed I/O (PIO) — the CPU is the data mover, consuming CPU cycles and producing
throughput numbers limited by the CPU’s PCIe write bandwidth rather than the fabric’s DMA
engine capacity.
The bandwidth test was replaced with a true DMA transfer: a 512 KB local SISCI segment is
created as the source buffer, a sci dma queue t is opened on the adapter, and SCIStartDmaTransfer
is called to move the data without CPU involvement. SCIWaitForDMAQueue blocks until the
hardware signals completion, providing an accurate transfer-complete timestamp. The resulting
bandwidth figure reflects the Dolphin card’s hardware DMA engine performance rather than
CPU-bottlenecked memory copies. PIO reads are retained for latency measurement, where
they remain appropriate: each volatile read across the fabric is a non-posted PCIe transaction
(request followed by completion packet), constituting one genuine round-trip.
2.4.4 Fabric Node ID Mismatch in GUI Polling Logic
The GUI monitoring system maintains live metric cards for all three nodes using a per-node
background polling thread that forks metrics reader at one-second intervals. An initial imple-
mentation of this polling thread passed the logical application-layer node indices (2, 3) directly
as Dolphin fabric node IDs.
The actual fabric node IDs in this system are 8 (DolphinBenny1) and 4 (DolphinBenny2),
assigned by the MXH930 DIP switch configuration. Attempting to connect to fabric IDs 2
and 3 either timed out or connected to nonexistent nodes, always returning an error result. The
polling thread then immediately called setActive(false) on the corresponding node card —
wiping out valid metrics data that had been written moments earlier by the correct code path,
causing the node cards to flash live data and revert to “OFFLINE” within the same display
refresh cycle.
The fix was to remove the incorrect polling path entirely and ensure all remote node con-
nections use the stored fabricNodeId field (8 or 4) from the NodeMetrics object rather than
any derived index.
2.4.5 Offline Detection Grace Period
A related issue affected the offline detection logic. The initial implementation marked a node
offline immediately upon any failed or slow poll. However, metrics reader has a non-trivial
maximum execution time: the SCIConnectSegment call was configured with a 5-second time-
out, the DMA SCIWaitForDMAQueue had a 5-second timeout, and Java’s process.waitFor()
imposed a 10-second ceiling. A slow but successful fetch could legitimately take 7–9 seconds
while still returning valid data.
Page 10
2 System Deployment and Integration Dolphin PCIe Benchmark
With an initial offline threshold of 3 seconds, a node was declared offline and its card grayed
out before the in-progress fetch had time to complete and return its data. The threshold was
raised to 15 seconds and the SCIConnectSegment timeout was simultaneously reduced to 2
seconds — providing a faster signal when a node is genuinely unreachable while giving in-
progress fetches sufficient time to complete.

3 Monitoring Dashboard: An Applied SISCI Demonstration
To demonstrate the practical utility of the SISCI API beyond synthetic benchmarks, a JavaFX
monitoring dashboard was developed that presents live performance telemetry from all three
fabric nodes in a single unified interface. The application, called the Dolphin Interconnect
Monitor, serves two roles simultaneously: it is a functional cluster monitoring tool, and it is a
demonstration of every major SISCI API capability working together in a real application.
3.1 Architecture
The monitoring system follows a publisher-subscriber architecture over the PCIe fabric. Each
remote node runs a persistent C process, metrics agent, which creates a 2 MB SISCI shared
memory segment (segment ID 500) and continuously writes a structured NodeMetricsData
record into it. This record contains CPU utilization (computed from a 200 ms /proc/stat
delta), total and available memory, per-mount storage usage, a 32-bit magic number (0xD01F1171)
for validity detection, and a millisecond-resolution timestamp.
The host node (ghost, fabric ID 12) runs two background processes. The metrics daemon
process connects to each remote node’s segment 500 every polling cycle and performs:
1. SCIConnectSegment + SCIMapRemoteSegment: Attaches to the remote node’s
metrics segment, then memcpys the full NodeMetricsData struct. This is a transparent
memory read — the application dereferences a regular pointer, and the PCIe fabric moves
the data.
2. PIO round-trip latency probe: Issues 1,000 volatile pointer reads to a reserved probe
address within the remote segment (PROBE OFFSET = 8 KB). The average elapsed time
across all iterations is reported as fabric round-trip latency in microseconds.
3. DMA bandwidth test: Allocates a 512 KB local SISCI segment, fills it with a test
pattern, and transfers it to the remote segment via SCIStartDmaTransfer. Throughput
is calculated as 512 KB
elapsed time (in GB/s).
Results are written to /tmp/dolphin node .json by metrics daemon. The JavaFX
GUI reads these files once per second via Platform.runLater, avoiding any SISCI calls on the
UI thread. A 15-second offline timeout prevents individual polling failures from falsely marking
nodes as unavailable.
3.2 Live Telemetry Dashboard

The header confirms fabric connectivity with the status line FABRIC STATUS: ALL 3 NODES
ACTIVE. Each node card displays CPU utilization, memory consumption, per-mount storage
usage, and, for the two remote nodes, live fabric latency and DMA bandwidth measured on the

3.3 Benchmark Control Panel
The right sidebar of the dashboard provides a Demo Controls panel with five buttons, each of
which invokes one of the benchmark programs described in Section 4:
• File Transfer — launches file transfer demo, which connects to segment 500 on Dol-
phinBenny1 and issues one or two concurrent DMA transfers (64 MB per queue) to report
transfer time and throughput in GB/s.
• Remote Memory — launches remote memory demo, which maps segment 500 on Dol-
phinBenny1, executes 1,000 PIO read iterations at the probe offset, and reports average,
minimum, maximum, and p99 latency in microseconds.
• Transparency Test — launches transparency demo, which maps segment 500 on Dol-
phinBenny1 and performs 100 write-flush-read cycles via plain C pointer dereferences,
measuring the latency of each complete cycle.
• Interrupt Demo — launches interrupt demo sender, which triggers 100 hardware
interrupts to interrupt demo receiver running on DolphinBenny1 and measures the
round-trip latency for each echo. The receiver connects dynamically by reading the
sender’s fabric ID from the interrupt payload.
• Fabric Drive — mounts a FUSE-based virtual filesystem (dolphin fuse) backed by
PCIe fabric memory at /tmp/dolphin-fabric. The drive stays mounted for 90 seconds
with a live countdown, then auto-unmounts via fusermount -u. No root privileges are
required.
Results for each demo are displayed inline under their respective button immediately upon
completion. This design allows a live operator to trigger each benchmark directly from the GUI
and see the result in context alongside the real-time telemetry.
The monitoring dashboard therefore serves as the primary user-facing demonstration: it
shows SISCI transparent memory reads, PIO latency probing, and DMA bandwidth measure-
ment running continuously in the background, while giving the operator on-demand access to
the deeper benchmark suite through the control panel.
4 Benchmark Methodology
Note: System architecture, hardware specifications, and configuration details are documented
in the companion Architecture Design document and in Section 2 of this report. This section
focuses exclusively on benchmark methodology and measurement techniques.
4.1 Test Environment
All benchmarks were executed on the three-node star topology described in Section 1. Node
roles during testing:
• ghost (Node 1, fabric ID 12) — benchmark controller; runs all demo programs and the
JavaFX monitoring GUI
• DolphinBenny1 (Node 2, fabric ID 8) — primary remote target for all benchmarks;
runs metrics agent and interrupt demo receiver as pre-requisite daemons
• DolphinBenny2 (Node 3, fabric ID 4) — secondary remote node; monitored by GUI;
not the target in single-target benchmarks

4 Benchmark Methodology Dolphin PCIe Benchmark
Test conditions:
• All non-essential services stopped to minimize interference
• Consistent system state across all test runs
• Each benchmark executed a minimum of five times to verify repeatability
• metrics agent running on Node 2 and Node 3 throughout (provides background SISCI
activity typical of operational conditions)
4.2 Benchmark Applications Overview
Five C programs compiled with -O2 optimization exercise distinct SISCI API capabilities:
4.2.1 File Transfer Demo (FTD)
• Purpose: Evaluate hardware DMA bulk transfer performance
• Transfer Size: 128 MB
• Mechanism: SCIStartDmaTransfer with a locally-mapped SISCI segment as source
• Metrics: Transfer time (ms), throughput (GB/s and MB/s), CPU overhead
4.2.2 Remote Memory Demo (RMD)
• Purpose: Characterize fine-grained RDMA latency
• Iterations: 1,000 PIO read operations (plus 10 warmup reads)
• Target: Remote node’s metrics agent segment (segment ID 500, 2 MB), read at a
reserved probe offset (8 KB)
• Timing: gettimeofday() with microsecond precision
• Metrics: Average, minimum, maximum, and 99th percentile latency
4.2.3 Transparency Demo (TD)
• Purpose: Assess transparent shared memory model overhead
• Iterations: 100 write-flush-read operation cycles
• Target: Remote node’s metrics agent segment (segment ID 500), accessed via SCIMapRemoteSegment
at probe offset (8 KB)
• Operation Sequence: Remote write →SCIFlush →remote read via plain pointer
dereference
• Metrics: Average time per complete operation cycle

4 Benchmark Methodology Dolphin PCIe Benchmark
4.2.4 Interrupt Demo (ID)
• Purpose: Measure hardware interrupt signaling round-trip latency
• Iterations: 100 interrupt round-trips
�� Mechanism: SCITriggerDataInterrupt (sender) / SCIWaitForDataInterrupt (receiver)
• Prerequisite: interrupt demo receiver running on Node 2 before test start
• Timing: clock gettime(CLOCK MONOTONIC) with nanosecond precision
• Metrics: Average, minimum, maximum, and 99th percentile round-trip latency
4.2.5 Fabric Drive (FD)
• Purpose: Demonstrate POSIX filesystem semantics over PCIe fabric shared memory
• Mechanism: FUSE-based virtual filesystem (dolphin fuse) backed by a local SISCI
segment; mounted at /tmp/dolphin-fabric
• Duration: Remains mounted for 90 seconds with a live countdown, then auto-unmounts
via fusermount -u
• Validation: Successful mount, standard file operations (open/read/write/close) via the
VFS path, and clean unmount without root privileges
• Note: This demo validates functionality rather than producing quantitative throughput
or latency metrics
4.3 Measurement Techniques
4.3.1 Timing Methodology
• High-resolution gettimeofday() or clock gettime() calls for microsecond/nanosecond-
precision timing
• Measurements captured immediately before and after critical operations
• Minimal logging during timed sections to avoid measurement interference
• All timestamps recorded in microseconds for consistent analysis
4.3.2 Statistical Analysis
Where applicable, the following statistics are computed from measurement data:
• Mean (Average): Central tendency across all measurements
• Minimum: Best-case performance observed
• Maximum: Worst-case performance observed
• 99th Percentile (p99): Tail latency characterization for predictability assessment
• Standard Deviation: Consistency and variability analysis (where computed)
Page 16
4 Benchmark Methodology Dolphin PCIe Benchmark
4.4 Data Collection and Analysis
All benchmarks output structured JSON format containing:
• Success/failure status
• Primary performance metrics (latency, throughput)
• Timing measurements
• Error codes and diagnostic information
JSON output enables automated result parsing, consistent formats across all benchmarks,
and reproducible result verification. Results are also recorded in per-demo CSV files (results/*.csv)
for aggregation and graph generation.
4.5 Test Execution Procedure
Standard procedure for each benchmark run:
1. Verify Dolphin fabric connectivity: dis diag, disinfo -hostnames
2. Confirm all five SISCI services running on each node
3. Start metrics agent on Node 2 and Node 3 (if not already running)
4. For Interrupt Demo: start interrupt demo receiver on Node 2
5. Launch benchmark from ghost (Node 1) via GUI or command line
6. Capture JSON output; verify successful completion via exit code
7. Record any anomalies or errors
8. Repeat for a minimum of five runs

5.1.3 Analysis
The file transfer benchmark demonstrates the raw bandwidth capabilities of the Dolphin PCIe
interconnect using hardware DMA offload:
• Consistent Throughput: All five runs produced throughput between 7.159 and 7.167 GB/s,
with an overall mean of 7.163 GB/s and a run-to-run standard deviation of only 0.004 GB/s,
demonstrating stable per-link DMA bandwidth.
• Link-Independent Throughput: Run 4, conducted at 64 MB over a single x4 link,
achieved the same 7.159 GB/s as the 128 MB dual-link runs, confirming that the measured
bandwidth reflects the per-link DMA ceiling rather than an aggregate across both links.
• CPU Offload: Hardware DMA allows the CPU to remain free during the transfer; the
only CPU cost is DMA queue setup and the final SCIWaitForDMAQueue synchronization.
• Transfer Granularity: Each DMA queue issues one contiguous 64 MB transfer. In
dual-queue mode, two queues are submitted before either is awaited, giving the NTB
hardware the opportunity to stripe across both x4 links simultaneously.
The achieved mean throughput of 7.163 GB/s corresponds to approximately 57.3 Gbps of
effective data movement per link, with the five recorded runs remaining tightly clustered around
that mean.

5.2.3 Analysis
The remote memory access benchmark reveals the following performance characteristics:
• Low Average Latency: All five runs recorded average latencies between 1.589 and
1.773 µs, a range of 0.184 µs, with a run-to-run standard deviation of 0.076 µs. Run 2
was notably the lowest at 1.589 µs, likely benefiting from a warm TLB and cache state.
• Floor Latency: The minimum observed latency of 1.000 µs across all runs represents
the best-case PCIe round-trip for a single PIO read.
• Stable Tail Latency: The p99 latency was consistently 2.000 µs across every run,
indicating that nearly all operations complete within 2 µs with no run-to-run variation in
the tail.
• Outlier Spikes: Maximum latencies up to 23.000 µs occur in isolated iterations, most
likely due to OS scheduling preemption or transient cache effects during the volatile pointer
dereference.
The measured average latency of 1.724 µs is well below typical network round-trips by more
than an order of magnitude, confirming the suitability of Dolphin PIO reads for distributed
shared-memory access patterns.

5.3.3 Operation Breakdown
Each of the 100 test cycles consists of three sub-operations accessed through a plain C pointer
after SCIMapRemoteSegment:
1. Remote Write: Write a 32-bit value to the probe offset within segment 500
2. Flush: SCIFlush ensures the write is visible on the remote node
3. Remote Read: Volatile pointer dereference reads the value back from the remote segment
Page 22
5 Experimental Results Dolphin PCIe Benchmark
Figure 5: Breakdown of time spent in each operation type
5.3.4 Analysis
The transparent memory access benchmark demonstrates the performance characteristics of the
SISCI shared memory programming model:
• Consistent Performance: All five runs completed between 1.950 and 2.020 µs per cycle,
with a mean of 1.978 µs and low run-to-run variability (std dev 0.029 µs).
• Flush Cost: Each cycle includes a full SCIFlush to guarantee write visibility on the
remote node. That the total cycle time (write + flush + read) remains approximately
2 µs on average demonstrates how efficiently the hardware pushes writes through the PCIe
fabric.
• Mixed Access Pattern: Combining a write, a coherence barrier, and a read in under
2.1 µs on average shows the transparent model is viable for applications that require
bidirectional shared-memory communication.
• Developer Convenience: Plain C pointer semantics mean no explicit SISCI DMA or
PIO API calls are required inside the hot path, significantly reducing code complexity
relative to explicit RDMA.
With a mean cycle time of 1.978 µs across three sub-operations, the transparent model
imposes only modest overhead compared to a single explicit PIO read (1.724 µs), making it an
attractive choice for rapid prototyping and applications that prioritise code simplicity.

The Interrupt Demo characterizes the round-trip latency of Dolphin’s hardware interrupt mech-
anism, in which one node triggers a data interrupt on a remote node and measures the time until
an echo interrupt is received back. This benchmark exercises SCITriggerDataInterrupt and
SCIWaitForDataInterrupt, the SISCI calls responsible for asynchronous cross-fabric signaling.

The interrupt benchmark provides the most direct measurement of the fabric’s signaling la-
tency — distinct from the data-transfer latency measured by the Remote Memory Demo. Be-
cause an interrupt carries no data payload, the result isolates the overhead of the SISCI in-
terrupt notification path: the PCIe Message Signaled Interrupt (MSI/MSI-X) write on the
sending side, kernel driver dispatch on the receiving side, the user-space wakeup through
SCIWaitForDataInterrupt, and then the round-trip echo path back.
Key observations:
• Average RTT: The steady-state average RTT of 30.688 µs (runs 2–5) is roughly 17.8×
higher than a single RDMA PIO read (1.724 µs). This is expected: the interrupt path
involves two kernel-mode wakeups and two PCIe interrupt writes, whereas a PIO read is
a direct hardware-mapped memory dereference.
• Best-Case Floor: The minimum observed RTT of 20 µs (runs 1 and 5) represents the
irreducible hardware latency when both nodes are already in an interrupt-wait state with
no scheduler preemption.
• P99 Variability: The p99 latency ranges between 360 and 436 µs across all runs (mean
397 µs), with no clear startup penalty — run 3 produced the highest p99 at 436 µs. This
run-to-run spread in the tail reflects OS scheduler activity on the receiver side.
• Sleep-Based Waiting: The receiver parks on SCIWaitForDataInterrupt, yielding the
CPU between rounds. This means the latency includes thread re-scheduling overhead on
the receiver side, which is the dominant source of variability. A polling-based receiver
would achieve lower and more consistent RTT at the cost of a dedicated CPU core.
• Application Use Case: Despite higher average latency than PIO reads, interrupt sig-
naling is the correct mechanism for producer-consumer synchronization, as it allows the
waiting node to sleep rather than spin-poll, making it suitable for event-driven workloads
where minimising CPU utilisation is more important than minimising wake-up latency.
6 Performance Analysis
This section provides a comprehensive analysis of the performance results, identifying key trends,
measured constraints, and practical implications for system design and application development.
Page 25
6 Performance Analysis Dolphin PCIe Benchmark
6.1 Performance Summary
The evaluation of the three-node Dolphin ICS system reveals distinct performance characteris-
tics across different usage patterns:
• Bulk Transfer (DMA): File transfers achieve 7.163 GB/s on average (peak 7.167 GB/s),
consistent with the PCIe 4.0 x4 per-link ceiling of∼7.88 GB/s following ghost’s CPU
upgrade
• Fine-Grained Access (RDMA): Remote memory operations exhibit 1.724 µs average
latency, suitable for latency-sensitive workloads
• Transparent Access: Operation cycle overhead of 1.978 µs per write-flush-read cycle
• Interrupt Signaling: Steady-state round-trip interrupt latency of 30.688 µs across 100
iterations
6.2 Performance Trade-offs
6.2.1 Bandwidth vs. Latency
The results demonstrate the classic bandwidth-latency trade-off in interconnect design:
• Large DMA transfers maximize bandwidth utilization
• Small RDMA operations prioritize latency over throughput
• Application requirements dictate optimal access pattern
6.2.2 Explicit vs. Transparent Access
Two programming models offer different benefits:
Table 14: Programming Model Comparison
Aspect Explicit RDMA Transparent Memory
Performance Higher Lower (overhead)
Complexity Higher Lower
Flexibility Maximum Constrained
Best For HPC, latency-critical Rapid development
6.2.3 Data Transfer vs. Interrupt Signaling
The interrupt RTT benchmark provides a complement to the RDMA latency measurement:
both exercise the same physical PCIe links but through fundamentally different paths. RDMA
read operations are non-posted PCIe transactions (request + completion), measured by the
CPU performing volatile memory reads across the fabric. Interrupt signaling uses MSI/MSI-X
writes and kernel-level interrupt dispatch on the receiving node. Comparing 1.724 µs average
RDMA latency against 30.688 µs steady-state interrupt RTT quantifies the relative overhead
of each signaling mechanism: interrupt dispatch costs approximately 17.8×more than a bare
PIO read, attributable to two kernel-mode wakeups and two PCIe MSI writes in the round-trip
path.
Page 26
6 Performance Analysis Dolphin PCIe Benchmark
6.3 Bottleneck Analysis
6.3.1 Hardware Bottlenecks
• PCIe Bandwidth: The star topology routes all inter-node traffic through ghost. DMA
transfers from ghost to either leaf node consume ghost’s PCIe bandwidth; simultaneous
transfers to both nodes would compete on ghost’s PCIe root complex bandwidth
• Memory Bandwidth: Local DRAM bandwidth on ghost is shared between the DMA
source buffer writes and any concurrent CPU operations
• PCIe 4.0 Per-Link Ceiling: Ghost was upgraded from its original Ryzen 3 3200G to a
Ryzen 7 3700, enabling PCIe 4.0 on the CPU-attached slot of the ASRock B550M Pro4,
which supports x4×4 bifurcation. All four ports of ghost’s MXH940 are active: ports 0–1
connect to DolphinBenny1, ports 2–3 connect to DolphinBenny2. Each x4 link has a
theoretical PCIe 4.0 ceiling of∼7.88 GB/s; the measured sustained DMA throughput of
∼7.16 GB/s represents∼91% link utilization
• Bandwidth Split Across Directions: Ghost’s total PCIe 4.0 bandwidth is divided
between two leaf nodes. An earlier target of∼16 GB/s (based on a full x8 connection to
a single node) proved unattainable: with x4×4 bifurcation, each direction receives only
two independent x4 links. Submitting two concurrent DMA queues (dual-queue mode)
was intended to saturate both x4 links to DolphinBenny1, but in practice the dual-queue
runs achieve the same∼7.16 GB/s as the single-queue run 4, indicating the bottleneck is
the NTB crossbar or the remote node’s PCIe interface — not the DMA submission count
on ghost
6.3.2 Software Bottlenecks
• API Overhead: SCIConnectSegment has a non-trivial setup time (observed up to 2 s in
worst case); not relevant for sustained transfers but significant for short-lived connections
• DMA Queue Management: SCICreateDMAQueue / SCIRemoveDMAQueue add setup
and teardown overhead around each transfer; amortized cost is low for large transfers but
observable for small ones
• Interrupt Dispatch: SCIWaitForDataInterrupt involves a kernel-level wait; scheduler
jitter on the receiving node contributes to p99 latency inflation in the interrupt benchmark
6.4 Scaling Considerations
6.4.1 Node Count Scaling
The current three-node star configuration provides insights into scaling behavior:
• All four MXH940 ports in use: Ghost’s B550M Pro4 with x4×4 bifurcation and the
Ryzen 7 3700 CPU has all four ports active — two to each leaf node. The current topology
fully utilises the card’s available connections. Adding a third leaf node to ghost would
require either a higher-port-count MXH940 variant or a switching-capable intermediate
node
• Ghost acts as a bandwidth bottleneck for simultaneous multi-node transfers; adding more
leaf nodes increases contention on ghost’s PCIe root complex
• Adding a switch-style node (multi-port MXH930 in forwarding mode) could relieve this
bottleneck and enable leaf-to-leaf direct paths
Page 27
6 Performance Analysis Dolphin PCIe Benchmark
• Configuration complexity grows linearly (one dishosts.conf entry and one ADAPTER block
per additional node)
6.4.2 Data Size Scaling
Performance characteristics vary with data size:
• Small transfers (KB): Latency-dominated, RDMA preferred
• Medium transfers (MB): Transition region, both approaches viable
• Large transfers (tens of MB): Throughput-dominated, DMA preferred
6.5 Application Suitability
Based on the performance characteristics observed, the Dolphin ICS system is well-suited for:
6.5.1 Recommended Applications
• Distributed Databases: Low-latency remote memory access for data sharing
• HPC Clusters: High-bandwidth inter-node DMA communication
• Real-Time Systems: Predictable 1.724 µs average RDMA latency with a consistent p99
of 2.000 µs across all five runs
• Event-Driven Systems: Low-overhead interrupt signaling for producer-consumer coor-
dination without polling
• Shared Memory Parallel Processing: Transparent programming model simplifies
development
6.5.2 Less Suitable Applications
• Applications requiring thousands of concurrent connections (SCIConnectSegment setup
cost)
• Workloads with predominantly tiny (<100 byte) messages not amortizing DMA setup
• Applications deployed on consumer hardware with PCIe BAR constraints that prevent
installation (see Section 2)

6.7 Optimization Recommendations
Based on the evaluation results, the following optimizations are recommended:
Page 28
7 Conclusions and Recommendations Dolphin PCIe Benchmark
1. For Maximum Bandwidth: Use DMA transfers for data >1 MB
2. For Minimum Latency: Use explicit RDMA with sizes <4 KB
3. For Development Speed: Use transparent memory model and optimize later if needed
4. For CPU Efficiency: Leverage DMA (not PIO/memcpy) to offload transfers from CPU
5. For Predictability: Monitor p99 latency, not just averages
6. For Event Signaling: Use interrupts rather than polling where receiver can block
7 Conclusions and Recommendations
This performance evaluation has provided both a practical deployment account and empirical
characterization of the three-node Dolphin PCIe fabric system through benchmarking across
five performance domains. The combined narrative of challenges overcome and benchmarks
measured offers a complete view of deploying SISCI-based systems on consumer-class hardware
outside traditional datacenter environments.
7.1 Summary of Deployment Findings
Section 2 documented the key integration challenges:
• Consumer-class Windows machines are incompatible with the MXH930 due to PCIe BAR
resource conflicts that their BIOS cannot resolve (This claim is only based on the findings
in this project so far, there may be a solution I have yet to find); Linux’s pci=realloc
parameter makes the identical hardware work reliably
• GRUB bootloader heap corruption from BAR collision is resolved with the same pci=realloc
parameter
• The Dolphin driver installer requires --skip-distro-check on HWE kernels
• The dishosts.conf parser silently ignores entries that appear after a SOCKETADAPTER
block, making configuration ordering a non-obvious but critical requirement
• From first hardware insertion to stable three-node operation: eleven days (March 10–21,
2026), with the majority spent on the failed Windows compatibility investigation
7.2 Summary of Empirical Findings
The benchmark measurements demonstrate the following performance characteristics:
1. DMA Bulk Transfer (FTD): Achieved 7.163 GB/s average throughput (peak 7.167 GB/s),
consistent with the PCIe 4.0 x4 per-link ceiling of∼7.88 GB/s following ghost’s CPU up-
grade to a Ryzen 7 3700
2. RDMA Fine-Grained Access (RMD): Mean latency of 1.724 µs with a consistent
p99 of 2.000 µs across 1,000 PIO read operations — std dev 0.076 µs across five runs
3. Transparent Memory Model (TD): Average operation cycle time of 1.978 µs per
write-flush-read sequence across 100 cycles, only 0.254 µs above bare RDMA
4. Interrupt Signaling (ID): Steady-state average round-trip latency of 30.688 µs (best-
case floor 20 µs) across 100 iterations
Page 29
7 Conclusions and Recommendations Dolphin PCIe Benchmark
5. Fabric Drive (FUSE): Successfully mounted a POSIX-compliant virtual filesystem
backed by remote PCIe segment memory; remained accessible for the full 90-second win-
dow before clean auto-unmount
7.3 Measured Performance Characteristics
The recorded results establish the following performance characteristics for the implemented
system:
• RDMA Latency: The system delivered 1.724 µs mean RDMA latency, with a consistent
p99 of 2.000 µs across all five benchmark runs
• DMA Throughput: The system delivered 7.163 GB/s mean DMA throughput (peak
7.167 GB/s), approaching the PCIe 4.0 x4 per-link ceiling of∼7.88 GB/s
• CPU Overhead: DMA transfers offload data movement entirely to hardware; the CPU
is occupied only during SCIStartDmaTransfer submission and SCIWaitForDMAQueue syn-
chronization
• Reliability: 100% success rate across all 20 quantitative benchmark runs collected during
evaluation, plus successful Fabric Drive operation
7.4 Performance Optimization Insights
Based on empirical measurements, the following optimization strategies are recommended:
7.4.1 When to Use Each Approach
• DMA Transfers: Optimize for bulk data movement >1 MB
• Explicit RDMA (PIO reads): Best for latency-critical operations accessing small
regions
• Transparent Model: Suitable for rapid prototyping with only 0.254 µs overhead over
explicit RDMA (1.978 µs vs 1.724 µs)
• Interrupt Signaling: Optimal for event-driven producer-consumer patterns where re-
ceiver can block
7.4.2 Identified Bottlenecks
Empirical testing revealed the following performance considerations:
• Star topology concentrates all inter-leaf traffic through ghost; simultaneous multi-node
DMA would contend on ghost’s PCIe root complex
• SCIConnectSegment setup time (up to 2 s) dominates for programs that establish and
tear down connections per operation
• Kernel scheduler jitter contributes to p99 inflation in interrupt RTT measurements
Page 30
7 Conclusions and Recommendations Dolphin PCIe Benchmark
7.5 Practical Deployment Recommendations
For researchers and developers implementing SISCI-based systems on consumer hardware:
1. Use Linux: Consumer BIOS PCIe BAR management is incompatible with the MXH930
on Windows; Linux with pci=realloc is the only viable OS for this hardware combination
2. Add pci=realloc swiotlb=65536: These kernel parameters are required for stable boot
with the MXH930 installed; add them before first boot with the card present
3. Verify dishosts.conf block ordering: HOSTNAME/ADAPTER blocks must precede
all SOCKETADAPTER blocks; violations cause silent parse failures with no error output
4. Profile Before Optimization: Measure actual workload characteristics to select appro-
priate API approach
5. Monitor Tail Latency: Track p99 metrics, not just averages, for predictable perfor-
mance
6. Use Hardware DMA for Bulk Transfers: For transfers >1 MB, dedicated DMA
provides higher throughput and lower CPU involvement than PIO (CPU-side memcpy
into mapped remote address)
7.6 Measurement Limitations
This evaluation’s scope was constrained by:
• Topology: Star configuration only; direct leaf-to-leaf paths and multi-hop latency not
measured
• Node Count: Limited to three-node configuration; larger topologies may exhibit dif-
ferent scaling. Ghost’s ASRock B550M Pro4 with x4×4 bifurcation and the upgraded
Ryzen 7 3700 CPU has all four MXH940 ports active — two to each leaf node. All avail-
able ports are in use; adding a third leaf node would require a higher-port-count card or
a switch-capable intermediate node. The intended 4th candidate node (HP OmniDesk
M02-0127c) was excluded due to a consumer BIOS that provides no controls for PCIe
BAR assignment, making it incompatible with the MXH930 under any Windows or Linux
configuration without reinstalling the OS with the card pre-installed
• Single Configuration: Ghost was upgraded from a Ryzen 3 3200G to a Ryzen 7 3700
during the evaluation period, enabling PCIe 4.0 on the B550M Pro4’s CPU-attached
slot. The measured∼7.16 GB/s DMA throughput is consistent with the PCIe 4.0 x4
per-link ceiling of∼7.88 GB/s. An earlier bandwidth target of∼16 GB/s (based on a
theoretical x8 connection) was not achieved: with x4×4 bifurcation, ghost’s bandwidth is
split across both leaf-node directions, and the dual-queue DMA approach did not yield
additive throughput over a single queue in practice
• Workload Variety: Synthetic benchmarks may not reflect all application patterns
7.7 Future Performance Research
The empirical results suggest several directions for extended investigation:
1. Mesh Topology: Add direct leaf-to-leaf cables and measure the latency reduction vs.
star routing through ghost

7 Conclusions and Recommendations Dolphin PCIe Benchmark
2. Concurrent Load: Benchmark behavior under simultaneous multi-threaded DMA from
multiple nodes
3. Scaling Studies: Measure performance with 4, 8, and 16-node configurations
4. Application Profiles: Test real-world workloads (databases, ML training, simulation)
5. Windows Compatibility: Investigate whether reinstalling Windows with the card al-
ready present (NVMe at 04:00.0) produces a stable dual-boot configuration
7.8 Integration with Research Series
This performance evaluation completes the foundational research trilogy:
• Literature Review: Established theoretical context and technology background
• Architecture Design: Specified system configuration and expected operating charac-
teristics
• Performance Evaluation: Documented deployment reality and measured system be-
havior through empirical benchmarking
The combination of deployment documentation and measured performance data provides a
complete picture of what it takes to operate Dolphin PCIe fabric technology on consumer-class
hardware: the practical prerequisites are non-trivial but surmountable, and once operational,
the system delivers stable low-latency and high-bandwidth communication across the evalu-
ated workloads. Results demonstrate practically significant performance across all measured
domains: DMA bulk-transfer throughput of 7.163 GB/s (approaching the PCIe 4.0 x4 per-link
ceiling of∼7.88 GB/s), RDMA latency of 1.724 µs (consistent p99 = 2.000 µs), and a 100%
benchmark success rate across all 20 quantitative runs — collectively supporting the viability
of community-scale deployments as proposed in the literature review.
7.9 Concluding Remarks
Empirical benchmarking of the three-node Dolphin ICS system has quantified practical per-
formance characteristics across DMA bulk transfer, fine-grained RDMA, transparent memory
access, and interrupt signaling. The deployment account in Section 2 provides equally impor-
tant practical guidance: the Linux-only requirement, the pci=realloc kernel parameter, the
dishosts.conf ordering constraint, and the DMA-vs.-PIO distinction are all lessons that are
not documented in Dolphin’s official materials but are essential for successful deployment on
non-datacenter hardware. Future work should extend these measurements to mesh topologies
and larger configurations to fully characterize the technology’s capabilities at scale.
